research_text:
## 1. What the finding refers to

`java.security.KeyStore` provides access to a provider-backed storage facility for cryptographic keys and certificates. Entries are identified by aliases and can include private keys, secret keys, and trusted certificates. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

The reported `InvalidSequenceOfMethodCalls` concerns the **modeled order of API calls**, not a particular key, certificate, password, or persisted value. The supplied detector description says the sequence is tracked per `KeyStore` object. The CrySL file itself defines the event order quoted below, but does not identify the detector version, its object-tracking implementation, or the actual calls behind this finding. A reported call also does not by itself establish that it returned successfully. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl))

Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl

## 2. Documented usage and remediation

Oracle documents that a keystore must be loaded before access **unless it was already loaded during instantiation**. For a type-based instance, `load` initializes it; passing a null input stream creates an empty keystore. The file-based `getInstance` overloads return an already-loaded keystore. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

The API documents reading entries with `getEntry` or keys with `getKey`, and writing through methods including `setEntry`, `setKeyEntry`, and `setCertificateEntry`. It does **not** prescribe the CrySL rule’s universal pattern of following every `getEntry` with `getKey`, or every `setEntry` with `store`. For example, Android’s official documentation shows loading `AndroidKeyStore` and reading a private-key entry with `getEntry` without a following `getKey`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))

For safety, the documented behavior matters:

- If no password is supplied for integrity checking during `load`, integrity checking is not performed. `getKey` can return null or throw if recovery fails; a call alone does not establish successful recovery. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))
- Persistence and its mechanism are provider-dependent. An AOSP implementation at the cited revision rejects `store(OutputStream, char[])`; that implementation is not evidence about every Android version or provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))
- `PasswordProtection.destroy()` clears its stored password; the caller is responsible for clearing any clones it creates. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.PasswordProtection.html))

**Remediation documented by the API:** initialize before access when necessary, use the provider’s supported operations and protection parameters, and handle loading and recovery failures. The official API sources do not prescribe a single remediation for a CrySL sequence finding. In particular, they do not recommend mechanically adding calls solely to satisfy this rule.

Sources: https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.PasswordProtection.html

## 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Stored formats:** Oracle says the keystore type determines storage format and protection algorithms; implementations of different types are generally incompatible. PKCS12 is the recommended default in JDK 9 and later. Oracle advises migrating JKS and JCEKS to PKCS12 with `keytool -importkeystore`; the tool documents importing one or all entries between stores. Compatibility still depends on the providers and entries involved. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html?source=:ow:lp:cpo::))
- **Wire formats:** The cited `KeyStore` documentation does not define a wire-format change resulting from changing call order. PKCS12 is documented as a portable storage/transport format, not as a guarantee of compatibility with every consumer. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html?source=%3Aow%3Alp%3Acpo%3A%3A&utm_source=openai))
- **Platform versions:** Both file-based `getInstance` overloads are documented since Java 9 and Android API level 33. Android documents its Keystore provider feature from API level 18. Provider and type availability must be checked for the target platform. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyStore.html))
- **Changing only call order:** No general persisted-data or wire-format migration is specified for that change. Whether a particular usage change affects stored data depends on the operations and provider; the supplied finding does not establish those details.

Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/24/docs/specs/man/keytool.html

## 4. What the referenced CrySL source states

The source declares `SPEC java.security.KeyStore`. Its **event declarations have argument lists**; they are not unconstrained method-name-only patterns:

| Event | Declared call shape |
|---|---|
| `Get` | `getInstance(type)` or `getInstance(type, _)`; `type` is declared `String` |
| `Load` | `load(fileInput, passwordIn)` or `load(paramLoad)`; declared types are `InputStream`, `char[]`, and `LoadStoreParameter` |
| `GetEntry` | `getEntry(aliasGet, protParamGet)`; `String`, `ProtectionParameter` |
| `GetKey` | `key = getKey(alias, passwordKey)`; `String`, `char[]`; result declared `Key` |
| `SetEntry` | `setEntry(aliasSet, entry, protParamSet)`; `String`, `KeyStore.Entry`, `ProtectionParameter` |
| `Store` | `store(paramStore)` or `store(fileOutput, passwordOut)`; `LoadStoreParameter`, or `OutputStream`, `char[]` |

The exact **order clause** is: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl))

```text
ORDER
	Get, Load, ((GetEntry?, GetKey) | (SetEntry, Store))*
```

Thus the stated order begins with `Get`, then `Load`, followed by zero or more read branches—optional `GetEntry` then `GetKey`—or write branches of `SetEntry` then `Store`. Separately, the file lists five uppercase type values and password-related constraints; these are distinct from the `ORDER` clause. It does not list the file-based factories or several other documented `KeyStore` methods. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyStore.crysl))

**Same-named methods:** The file scopes its events to `java.security.KeyStore`; it does not state a name-only rule covering unrelated receiver types. However, it contains no separate matcher implementation or formal clause specifying how a detector resolves receivers, overloads, `_`, or unresolved calls. **From this file alone, whether a particular detector could match an unrelated method that merely shares a name cannot be determined.**

**Source limits:** The URL points to a mutable branch. The supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified against an immutable revision, and the detector release and configuration remain unknown. Review of the actual resolved calls and detector behavior is therefore necessary; this brief does not determine whether the finding is valid for any particular code.
